card.chief_complaint: pressure-like chest pain at rest with sweating

ask.changes_what: Positive: raise pretest probability for ACS and proceed promptly to ECG/troponin pathway. Negative: no change; ACS remains in play.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of radiation or sweating to lower suspicion; do not apply to patients with aortic dissection features (tearing pain, pulse deficit) where arm symptoms have a different meaning.
ask.escalation_warning: Bilateral-arm radiation with diaphoresis is a high-probability ACS pattern: immediate ECG, troponin, aspirin unless contraindicated, and monitored bed.

evidence.citation: Fanaroff AC, Rymer JA, Goldstein SA, Simel DL, Newby LK. Does This Patient With Chest Pain Have Acute Coronary Syndrome? The Rational Clinical Examination Systematic Review. JAMA. 2015;314(18):1955-1965.
evidence.population: ED patients with chest pain suggestive of ACS (prospective studies 1995-2015)
evidence.quote: pain radiation to both arms (specificity, 96%; LR, 2.6 [95% CI, 1.8-3.7])
evidence.reference_standard: Final hospital diagnosis of ACS or cardiovascular event within 6 weeks

evidence.citation: Panju AA, Hemmelgarn BR, Guyatt GH, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient having a myocardial infarction? JAMA. 1998;280(14):1256-1263.
evidence.population: Patients with acute chest pain (studies summarised in the 1998 RCE)
evidence.quote: chest pain radiating to both the left and right arm simultaneously (LR, 7.1)
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of MI per included studies (ECG/enzymes)

evidence.citation: Goodacre S, Locker T, Morris F, Campbell S. How useful are clinical features in the diagnosis of acute, undifferentiated chest pain? Acad Emerg Med. 2002;9(3):203-208.
evidence.population: 893 ED chest pain unit patients with acute undifferentiated chest pain; 3.8% AMI
evidence.quote: pain radiating to the shoulder or both arms (LR = 4.07)

evidence.citation: Bruyninckx R, Aertgeerts B, Bruyninckx P, Buntinx F. Signs and symptoms in diagnosing acute myocardial infarction and acute coronary syndrome: a diagnostic meta-analysis. Br J Gen Pract. 2008;58(547):105-111.
evidence.population: Non-selected patients with chest pain (16 of 28 studies; primary care and ED)
evidence.quote: Sweating had the highest pooled positive likelihood ratio (LR+), namely 2.92 (95% CI = 1.97 to 4.23) for acute myocardial infarction

ask.how: Ask where the pain travels and have the patient point: to the left arm only, the right arm/shoulder, or both arms. Separately ask about, and look for, sweating at the time of pain (observed diaphoresis carries more weight than reported).
ask.negative_finding: Absence of bilateral-arm radiation or sweating is common in ACS and barely lowers the probability.
ask.pitfalls: Left-arm-only radiation adds little. The high 7.1 estimate comes from older MI cohorts and is not reproduced in the 2015 pooled ACS analysis; do not treat as diagnostic.
ask.positive_finding: Radiation to both arms is specific for ACS (pooled specificity 96%, LR 2.6) and for MI (LR 7.1 in the 1998 RCE); observed sweating has pooled LR+ 2.9 for AMI.
ask.prerequisites: Reliable history; record radiation site before the ECG result biases the interviewer.
ask.rationale: Radiation to both arms with diaphoresis strongly supports ACS and would prompt immediate ECG/troponin.
ask.title: Chest pain radiating to both arms (or right arm/shoulder), with diaphoresis

ask.changes_what: Positive: escalate to ADD-RS assessment, CXR/D-dimer and CT angiography as appropriate; negative onset lowers but does not eliminate dissection probability.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use gradual onset alone to exclude dissection in patients with other high-risk features (Marfan/aortic disease, pulse deficit, neurologic deficit, new murmur, hypotension).
ask.escalation_warning: Abrupt severe chest/back pain with hypotension, pulse deficit, or neurologic deficit is a dissection or ruptured AAA until proven otherwise: immediate CT angiography and surgical notification.

evidence.citation: Klompas M. Does this patient have an acute thoracic aortic dissection? JAMA. 2002;287(17):2262-2272.
evidence.population: Consecutive patients with confirmed thoracic aortic dissection from 21 studies (case series; sensitivity pooled; LR- derived from comparison cohorts)
evidence.quote: sudden onset (sensitivity, 84%). The absence of sudden pain onset lowers the likelihood of dissection (negative likelihood ratio [LR], 0.3; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.2-0.5)
evidence.reference_standard: Dissection confirmed by imaging, surgery, or autopsy
evidence.target_condition: Acute thoracic aortic dissection (finding: sudden-onset pain)

evidence.citation: Ohle R, Um J, Anjum O, et al. High risk clinical features for acute aortic dissection: a case-control study. Acad Emerg Med. 2018;25(4):378-384.
evidence.population: Matched case-control: 194 ED/in-hospital CT- or echo-confirmed AAD cases vs 776 ED controls with truncal pain <14 days and no clear diagnosis
evidence.quote: Absence of abrupt-onset pain (sensitivity = 95.9%, negative likelihood ratio = 0.07 [0.03-0.14]) can help rule out AAD.
evidence.reference_standard: CT angiography or echocardiography confirmed dissection

ask.how: Ask an open question about how the pain began, then specifically: 'Did it reach its worst within seconds, or build up over minutes?' Document time-to-peak intensity and whether the patient can pinpoint the moment of onset (what they were doing). Also ask about tearing/ripping quality and migration.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of sudden onset lowers the likelihood of dissection (LR- 0.3 in the RCE pooled series; 0.07 in an ED case-control study), but the clinical examination is insufficiently sensitive to rule out dissection on its own.
ask.pitfalls: Patients recall onset imprecisely, particularly after analgesia or when pain was preceded by exertion; gradual-onset presentations still occur in ~5-16% of dissections, especially in elderly patients or with painless neurologic presentations.
ask.positive_finding: Abrupt-onset pain is present in ~84-96% of aortic dissections but is common in other conditions, so it raises suspicion for dissection only modestly (specificity not established in unselected cohorts); it is a high-risk feature in the ADD risk score.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give history; otherwise ask witnesses or EMS about onset.
ask.rationale: Abrupt, maximal-onset pain would raise suspicion for aortic dissection and escalate to urgent imaging.
ask.title: Pain abrupt in onset and maximal at onset (thunderclap-type chest/back pain)

ask.changes_what: Positive: de-emphasize ACS and work up PE/pneumonia/pneumothorax/pericarditis (exam, CXR, PE risk score). Negative: does not remove PE from the differential.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use pleuritic quality to discharge a patient with possible ACS without an ECG and troponin.
ask.escalation_warning: Pleuritic pain with hypoxemia, tachycardia, unilateral leg swelling or hemoptysis warrants immediate PE work-up; with sudden dyspnea consider pneumothorax.

evidence.citation: Panju AA, Hemmelgarn BR, Guyatt GH, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient having a myocardial infarction? JAMA. 1998;280(14):1256-1263.
evidence.population: Adults with acute chest pain in studies pooled by the RCE review
evidence.reference_standard: Confirmed MI by study criteria (enzymes/ECG) in included studies

evidence.citation: Courtney DM, Kline JA, Kabrhel C, et al. Clinical features from the history and physical examination that predict the presence or absence of pulmonary embolism in symptomatic emergency department patients: results of a prospective, multicenter study. Ann Emerg Med. 2010;55(4):307-315.
evidence.population: 7,940 symptomatic US ED patients tested for PE (12 centers); mean age 49, 67% female
evidence.quote: those with an adjusted odds ratio (OR) greater than 1.5 included non-cancer-related thrombophilia (OR 1.99), pleuritic chest pain (OR 1.53)
evidence.reference_standard: Imaging-confirmed PE or DVT within 45 days
evidence.target_condition: Venous thromboembolism (PE or DVT) in ED patients evaluated for PE

ask.how: Ask whether the pain is sharp and clearly worse with a deep breath, cough or sneeze (not with exertion or palpation), and whether there has been any hemoptysis. Ask separately about onset, exertional relation and positional relief so the pleuritic quality is not conflated with other descriptors.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of pleuritic quality does not exclude PE, pericarditis or pneumonia; PE frequently presents with isolated dyspnea or collapse without pleuritic pain.
ask.pitfalls: Pleuritic pain lowers but does not exclude ACS; no history element alone permits discharge without testing. Patients may label any sharp pain as breath-related unless asked specifically about inspiration.
ask.positive_finding: Pleuritic pain lowers the probability of myocardial infarction (LR about 0.2) and shifts the differential toward pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pneumothorax, pericarditis and pleural disease. In ED patients evaluated for PE it modestly raises VTE probability (adjusted OR 1.5).
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; ask before analgesia if feasible.
ask.rationale: Pleuritic pain would shift focus toward PE or pericarditis and away from ACS.
ask.title: Pleuritic chest pain (sharp, worse with inspiration/cough), +/- hemoptysis

ask.changes_what: Positional pain lowers ACS probability but does not obviate ECG/troponin; sitting-forward relief prompts ECG for PR depression/ST elevation and echo for effusion.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use positional pain to withhold ECG and troponin in patients with risk factors, exertional component, or hemodynamic instability.
ask.escalation_warning: Positional pain with fever, pericardial rub, hypotension or a large effusion on POCUS needs urgent evaluation for tamponade or purulent pericarditis.

evidence.citation: Panju AA, Hemmelgarn BR, Guyatt GH, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient having a myocardial infarction? JAMA. 1998.
evidence.population: Adults presenting with acute chest pain; studies summarised in the JAMA RCE (mostly ED cohorts)
evidence.reference_standard: Myocardial infarction by serial ECG and cardiac enzymes per included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute myocardial infarction — finding PRESENT = positional chest pain

ask.how: Ask whether the pain changes with body position, movement, twisting or breathing, and specifically whether lying flat worsens and sitting up or leaning forward eases it. Distinguish this from exertional pain and from pain reproduced by palpation, which are recorded separately.
ask.negative_finding: Non-positional pain slightly increases ACS probability but is non-specific; the absence of positional change does not exclude pericarditis or chest-wall pain.
ask.pitfalls: An LR of 0.3 does not exclude ACS in a high-pretest patient, and post-infarction pericarditis and dissection can both be positional. Patient descriptions are inconsistent and the finding was defined variably across studies.
ask.positive_finding: Positional chest pain argues AGAINST myocardial infarction (LR 0.3 in the JAMA RCE; 0.2-0.3 across reviews) and favours pericarditis, musculoskeletal or esophageal causes; relief on sitting forward with worsening supine is the characteristic pericarditis pattern in ESC guidance.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to describe pain; ask before analgesia when possible.
ask.rationale: Positional pain relieved by leaning forward suggests pericarditis and would change the diagnostic approach.
ask.title: Pain that is positional (changes with posture; relieved leaning forward = pericarditis; ACS negative)

examine.changes_what: Rub present: treat as pericarditis criterion; get ECG, troponin, echo. Rub absent: still apply the other three criteria; do not use to discount pericarditis or tamponade.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use presence or absence of a rub to decide about tamponade; that decision rests on hemodynamics, pulsus paradoxus, JVP and echo.
examine.escalation_warning: Rub with hypotension, rising JVP, or pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg means possible tamponade: urgent echo and cardiology.
examine.how: Sit the patient forward, ask for full exhalation and a breath-hold, and listen with the diaphragm firmly at the left lower sternal border. A rub is a superficial scratchy or leathery sound, classically with up to three components (atrial systole, ventricular systole, early diastole); it may come and go, so re-auscultate several times over hours.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of a rub does not exclude pericarditis; rubs are intermittent and were not present in most patients in prospective pericarditis cohorts. Absence of a rub with a large effusion says nothing about tamponade.
examine.pitfalls: Pleural rubs (disappear with breath-hold) and crunching artefact from skin or hair mimic a pericardial rub. The rub often vanishes as effusion accumulates, so its disappearance may signal worsening rather than improvement.
examine.positive_finding: A rub is one of the four ESC diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis (chest pain, rub, ECG changes, new/worsening effusion; 2 of 4 required) and is regarded as highly specific, but no sensitivity/specificity against an independent reference standard was found.
examine.prerequisites: Quiet room; patient able to sit forward and hold expiration.
examine.rationale: A pericardial friction rub is a key finding for pericarditis and would prompt targeted workup.
examine.title: Pericardial friction rub (triphasic scratchy sound, LSB, leaning forward, end-expiration)

examine.changes_what: Positive: treat as high-risk exam feature, obtain emergent CT angiography and manage BP using the higher-reading arm. Negative: does not lower suspicion; proceed on history and risk score.
examine.contraindications: Avoid cuff on an arm with AV fistula, recent surgery or lymphedema.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use equal arm pressures to exclude dissection; do not interpret a differential in a patient with known subclavian stenosis, AV fistula or prior arm vascular surgery.
examine.escalation_warning: Inter-arm difference >20 mmHg with acute chest/back pain, syncope or neurologic deficit: emergent CTA and surgical notification; treat hypotension as possible tamponade or rupture.

evidence.citation: Klompas M. Does this patient have an acute thoracic aortic dissection? JAMA. 2002;287(17):2262-2272.
evidence.population: Pooled consecutive patients with confirmed thoracic aortic dissection from 21 studies (1966-2000)
evidence.quote: 31% have pulse deficits or blood pressure differentials
evidence.reference_standard: Confirmed dissection by imaging, surgery or autopsy in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute thoracic aortic dissection (pulse deficit OR blood pressure differential, composite finding)

evidence.citation: Klompas M. Does this patient have an acute thoracic aortic dissection? JAMA. 2002;287(17):2262-2272.
evidence.population: Pooled patients with suspected/confirmed thoracic aortic dissection in the RCE review
evidence.quote: pulse or blood pressure differentials and neurological deficits increase the likelihood of disease (positive LRs, 5.7 and 6.6-33.0, respectively)
evidence.reference_standard: Confirmed dissection by imaging, surgery or autopsy in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute thoracic aortic dissection (pulse deficit OR blood pressure differential, composite finding)

evidence.citation: Shibata T, et al. Characteristics of Inter-Arm Difference in Blood Pressure in Acute Aortic Dissection. J Nippon Med Sch. 2022;89(1).
evidence.population: Consecutive patients with chest and/or back pain and suspected acute cardiovascular disease with BP measured in both arms: 58 type A AAD vs 122 non-AAD (single center, Japan, retrospective)
evidence.quote: L-R >20 mm Hg (14% vs. 4%, p=0.029) were higher in the TAAD group
evidence.target_condition: Stanford type A acute aortic dissection (left-minus-right systolic BP >20 mmHg)

examine.how: Measure systolic BP in both arms with an appropriately sized cuff, ideally simultaneously or in rapid succession with the patient in the same position, and repeat once; record which arm is lower. A difference >20 mmHg systolic is the conventional positive threshold.
examine.negative_finding: Equal arm pressures do not exclude dissection; only a minority of dissections (about 31% for the composite finding, 14% for >20 mmHg in type A) show a differential, and type B dissection rarely does.
examine.pitfalls: Inter-arm differences >10-20 mmHg are common in the general and hypertensive population from subclavian atherosclerosis, so specificity in low-prevalence settings is limited. Sequential rather than simultaneous measurement and cuff-size errors create false differences.
examine.positive_finding: An inter-arm systolic difference >20 mmHg increases the likelihood of aortic dissection (pooled LR+ 5.7 for the composite pulse/BP differential; sensitivity 14% vs 4% in type A dissection vs non-dissection in one retrospective series). Left-lower-than-right patterns implicate brachiocephalic involvement.
examine.prerequisites: Both arms accessible; no dialysis fistula, lymphedema or prior arm vascular surgery on the measured side.
examine.rationale: A significant inter-arm BP difference is a high-risk sign for aortic dissection and would trigger urgent imaging.
examine.title: Inter-arm systolic BP difference >20 mmHg

examine.changes_what: Positive: shift toward musculoskeletal/zoster causes, but still obtain ECG (and troponin if any ACS risk). Negative: no meaningful change in ACS probability.
examine.contraindications: Recent chest trauma, sternotomy, or suspected rib fracture - palpate gently.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use reproducible tenderness to forgo ECG/troponin in patients with high pretest probability (known CAD, ECG changes, diaphoresis, arm radiation); do not use after trauma or in suspected PE, where wall tenderness is common and uninformative.
examine.escalation_warning: If the ECG is ischaemic or troponin is elevated, ignore the tenderness; a dermatomal rash or unilateral burning pain preceding a rash should prompt early antiviral treatment for zoster.

evidence.citation: Bruyninckx R, Aertgeerts B, Bruyninckx P, Buntinx F. Signs and symptoms in diagnosing acute myocardial infarction and acute coronary syndrome: a diagnostic meta-analysis. Br J Gen Pract. 2008;58(547):105-111.
evidence.location: Abstract, Results (PubMed abstract; full text not accessible)
evidence.population: Non-selected patients with chest pain (16 of 28 studies; primary care and ED populations pooled)
evidence.quote: Absence of chest-wall tenderness on palpation had a LR- of 0.23 (95% CI = 0.18 to 0.29).

evidence.citation: Goodacre S, Locker T, Morris F, Campbell S. How useful are clinical features in the diagnosis of acute, undifferentiated chest pain? Acad Emerg Med. 2002;9(3):203-208.
evidence.population: 893 consecutive patients with acute, undifferentiated chest pain at a UK ED chest pain unit (AMI 3.8%)
evidence.quote: pain radiating to the shoulder or both arms (LR = 4.07), and chest wall tenderness (LR = 0.3)
evidence.reference_standard: WHO criteria for AMI with 6-month follow-up

examine.how: Ask the patient to localise the pain, then press firmly over the sternum, costochondral junctions, ribs and parasternal muscles; ask whether the pressure reproduces the presenting pain exactly (not merely causes soreness). Inspect the tender area for a dermatomal vesicular rash (zoster) before attributing pain to the chest wall.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of reproducible tenderness is the norm in MI (present in ~92-94% of AMI/ACS) but is non-specific and barely raises the probability of ACS (LR+ ~1.5 or less).
examine.pitfalls: Partial or vague tenderness is common in ACS and PE, so insist on exact reproduction; PE and pericarditis can coexist with wall tenderness; a low-prevalence (primary care) setting is where the finding is most useful, whereas in a high-risk ED patient it should not stop the workup.
examine.positive_finding: Pain fully reproduced by chest-wall palpation lowers the probability of MI/ACS about four-fold (LR ~0.2-0.3; pooled 0.23), supporting a musculoskeletal cause, but only 5-10% of infarcts have this feature and it does not exclude ACS.
examine.prerequisites: Patient able to compare elicited pain with the presenting pain; ECG obtained regardless.
examine.rationale: Reproducible chest wall tenderness would shift the differential toward musculoskeletal causes.
examine.title: Chest pain fully reproduced by palpation of chest wall

examine.changes_what: Positive: treat as high-risk feature and obtain immediate CT angiography; alert vascular/cardiac surgery. Negative: no reassurance; proceed on history, CXR and risk score.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid vigorous carotid palpation in patients with carotid bruit or known carotid disease.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal pulse exam to exclude dissection; do not attribute a deficit to dissection without imaging when chronic PAD or prior vascular surgery explains it.
examine.escalation_warning: New pulse deficit with chest/back pain, syncope, hypotension or focal neurology: emergent CTA, surgical consultation, and withhold antithrombotics.

evidence.population: Pooled consecutive patients with confirmed thoracic aortic dissection from 21 studies (1966-2000)
evidence.quote: 31% have pulse deficits or blood pressure differentials
evidence.reference_standard: Confirmed dissection by imaging, surgery or autopsy in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute thoracic aortic dissection (pulse deficit OR blood pressure differential, composite finding)

evidence.citation: Klompas M. Does this patient have an acute thoracic aortic dissection? JAMA. 2002;287(17):2262-2272.
evidence.population: Pooled patients with suspected/confirmed thoracic aortic dissection in the RCE review
evidence.quote: pulse or blood pressure differentials and neurological deficits increase the likelihood of disease (positive LRs, 5.7 and 6.6-33.0, respectively)
evidence.reference_standard: Confirmed dissection by imaging, surgery or autopsy in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute thoracic aortic dissection (pulse deficit OR blood pressure differential, composite finding)

evidence.citation: Ohle R, Um J, Anjum O, et al. High Risk Clinical Features for Acute Aortic Dissection: A Case-Control Study. Acad Emerg Med. 2018;25(4):378-387.
evidence.population: 194 confirmed nontraumatic AAD cases vs 776 age/sex-matched controls with truncal pain (2 tertiary EDs + 1 cardiac referral center)
evidence.reference_standard: AAD confirmed by CT or echocardiography

evidence.citation: Hagan PG, Nienaber CA, Isselbacher EM, et al. The International Registry of Acute Aortic Dissection (IRAD): new insights into an old disease. JAMA. 2000;283(7):897-903.
evidence.population: 464 patients with confirmed acute aortic dissection, 12 international referral centers, 1996-1998
evidence.quote: aortic regurgitation and pulse deficit were noted in only 31.6% and 15.1% of patients, respectively
evidence.reference_standard: Confirmed acute aortic dissection (registry entry criteria)
evidence.target_condition: Acute aortic dissection (sensitivity only; registry of confirmed cases)

examine.how: Palpate both radial, both carotid and both femoral pulses simultaneously, comparing amplitude and timing side to side; a deficit is an absent or clearly weaker pulse on one side, or a new deficit compared with prior exams. Confirm with bilateral arm BP measurement if a radial asymmetry is suspected.
examine.negative_finding: Absent pulse deficit does not exclude dissection: only about 15-31% of confirmed dissections have a pulse or BP deficit, so sensitivity is poor.
examine.pitfalls: Chronic peripheral arterial disease, prior vascular surgery, subclavian stenosis and shock cause deficits without dissection. Deficits may be transient and fluctuate as the false lumen changes.
examine.positive_finding: A pulse deficit substantially increases the likelihood of acute aortic dissection (pooled LR+ 5.7 for pulse or BP differential; LR+ 31 with specificity 99% in a case-control study) and marks branch-vessel involvement.
examine.prerequisites: Access to both arms and groins; note prior vascular surgery, dialysis access or known peripheral arterial disease.
examine.rationale: A pulse deficit is a critical sign of aortic dissection and would escalate to immediate CT angiography.
examine.title: Pulse deficit / asymmetric radial, carotid or femoral pulses

ask.rationale: Radiation to both arms with diaphoresis strongly supports ACS and would prompt immediate ECG/troponin.
Abrupt, maximal-onset pain would raise suspicion for aortic dissection and escalate to urgent imaging.
Pleuritic pain would shift focus toward PE or pericarditis and away from ACS.
Positional pain relieved by leaning forward suggests pericarditis and would change the diagnostic approach.

A significant inter-arm BP difference is a high-risk sign for aortic dissection and would trigger urgent imaging.
Reproducible chest wall tenderness would shift the differential toward musculoskeletal causes.
A pulse deficit is a critical sign of aortic dissection and would escalate to immediate CT angiography.
